items.fromString: This work item is related to SHIPSTRAT-20

Agentic SDLC needs many things. Local Agentic SDLC benefits from a shared toolbox. We need pilot teams to push the limits of what's possible.

One thing we learned from in the pilots is that we do not yet have a platform like Ambient Code that manages the full Agentic SDLC lifecycle for us, and we are probably not ready mandate one platform to rule them all. All of these efforts -- the AI toolbox (HPSTRAT-7), and all-in pilots (HPSTRAT-8) -- are complementary.

This feature addresses a different part of the problem: what happens when you need agents to do things that are highly sensitive, genuinely complex, and cannot tolerate wrong answers?

Releasing OpenShift requires access to official Red Hat signing keys. Diagnosing a CI regression requires cross-referencing six different data systems in real time. Reverting a breaking change requires understanding blast radius across platforms. These tasks require curated context from live systems, safe tools that are tested and released together, and a fallback system for when agents get stuck at 3am.

The SHIP group delivers this through two complementary systems:

* *Chai Bot* is a hierarchical framework for matching just enough context with tested, safe tools to accomplish specific tasks. It handles context engineering (finding the right information from live systems), intelligence engineering (learning, evaluation, fallback for stuck agents), and orchestrated autonomous execution (scheduled tasks, remote workspaces, multi-agent workflows). Chai is the system you reach when the problem is complex enough to need real-time context from multiple systems.
* *Prow-based agentic infrastructure* provides a simple, flexible complement to Chai's autonomous execution. Lightweight Claude-in-CI workflows like the payload agent, {{/jira:solve}}, and bot review guardrails run as periodic or triggered Prow jobs using the shared {{claude-ai-helpers}} container image. These are easier to set up for straightforward CI tasks. The ai-helpers plugin framework (tracked in the HPNEX project under HPSTRAT-7) is the execution substrate that makes this possible.

Both draw on two disciplines identified by Anthropic as foundational to effective agents:

* *Context engineering* ([Effective context engineering for AI agents|https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents]): finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of the desired outcome. Not more context -- the right context.
* *Predictable, safe tools* ([Writing effective tools for agents|https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents]): tools designed for agents, not just API wrappers. Tested, namespaced, token-efficient, and released together so you know what you are running.

The essay "[Complex, autonomous, high stakes tool calling with Chai|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cUyj-QhqYYCjhwOKJ6HDOEYmSSw3EvPUxVo5i9RUHmo/edit?disco=AAAB94d6uLg&tab=t.82daccnu3f2e]" explains the full rationale, including why these types of agents need context that is a byproduct of how we already work rather than a separate write-and-register effort.

h2. Status as of 2026Q2

This feature delivers proven workflows, some of which are already in production.  They fill the gap between what individual engineers can do on their own laptops and what requires centralized, tested infrastructure at organizational scale.

h2. Stats for the curious

* Chai Bot answers approximately hundreds of questions per day across dozens of Slack channels, serving teams across SHIP, ART, TRT, Test Platform, Konflux, HyperShift, ROSA, Quay, ACM, OpenShift AI, and others.
* Dozens of personas are configured and running, each with team-specific knowledge sources and some with team-specific tools and access controls.  You can see the full list [here|https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/docs/T027F3GAJ/F0BC4DY556V].
* 18 contributors across multiple teams.
* Teams outside SHIP are independently creating Jira issues to adopt Chai (APPSRE-14621 through 14627, ITPC-2328 through 2366, PLATENG-113, PERFSCALE-5100).
* The payload analysis agent helped improve the 5.0 nightly acceptance rate from 49% to 71%.
* ART prepared five payloads for release in a single day through Chai.

h3. *Feature Overview*

We want to significantly increase the likelihood of having an accepted nightly build every night in order to integrate OpenShift code more quickly into downstream processes such as Component Readiness and partner testing
h3. *Goals*
 * Remove a lot of noise from the CI signal that contributes to high number of nightly failures.
 * Reduce the time from PR merged to accepted nightly by a few hundred percent.
 * Increase visibility into the pipeline that produces accepted nightly payloads (art->crt->dptp->trt) 
 * Get ECs and RCs "for free" as a by-product of our normal nightly CI process.
 * A process that forces us to get slightly better whenever we fail (think mini-retro within SHIP)

h3. *Requirements*
 * We cannot reduce the effectiveness of Component Readiness in any significant way.
 * The end result must be _less_ work for SHIP engineers.

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*
h3. *Out of Scope*
 * My initial thought it to only consider changes that we have direct control over in SHIP.  There is a fuzzy line however.  We have done many things in SHIP that have improved product code quality.

h3. *Background*

Take a moment to browse the amd64 payload stream for the development version of OpenShift.  [Here's the link to 4.21|https://sippy.dptools.openshift.org/sippy-ng/release/4.21/streams/amd64/nightly/overview].  At the time of this writing we haven't had an accepted nightly in 6 days.

A reasonable person would panic if the saw this data, however, most people don't know the higher level process we use to ensure the work of hundreds of engineers continues to make OpenShift better every release.  The reality is, the engineering we've put into [Component Readiness|https://sippy.dptools.openshift.org/sippy-ng/component_readiness/main?view=4.21-main] has made it so that we haven't needed to rely on nightly builds as our primary signal for quality.

That said, there are several downstream processes that rely on nightly quality.
 * Accepted nightlies set the new baseline for periodics.  This is the data that feeds Component Readiness.
 * Every sprint we select a payload for our Engineering Candidate.  This is a public release that partners other dependent teams rely on.
 * By upgrading a portion of our our own critical infrastructure to Engineering Candidates, we'd caught no shortage of bugs that slipped through every other form of testing we have.
 * After branching we generate release candidates from accepted nightlies.

Going long periods of time without accepted nightlies generates ad-hoc communication throughout SHIP. 
 * Without accepted nightlies the last week of the sprint, the TRT has to scramble to find some way to manually accept a nightly.  This happens often and usually involved 5+ people talking for ~30 minutes plus an engineer or two going off on a special mission to debug an urgent but not important problem.
 * One reason it's urgent is that, without ECs, Product Managers come to ART asking which payload contains a feature they want to preview and if it could be made public.

h3. {*}Ideas (in no particular order):{*}{*}{*}
 * Dramatically increasing nightly build frequency to give us more chances for success
 * Removing low value testing from nightlies
 * Moving more testing to CI payloads (could improve Component Readiness speed)
 * Having a convenient “retry all tests for this payload”
 * Having more advanced ways to revert to the Last Known Good point in time and giving the freedom to fix the problem according to their schedule.
 * Keep identifying and eliminating sources of instability in our CI platform.  We have better data than ever for doing this.

A reasonable person would panic if the saw this data, however, most people don't know the higher level process we use to ensure the work of hundreds of engineers continues to make OpenShift better every release.  The reality is, the engineering we've put into [Component Readiness|https://sippy.dptools.openshift.org/sippy-ng/component_readiness/main?view=4.21-main] has made it so that we haven't needed to rely on nightly builds as our primary signal for quality.

That said, there are several downstream processes that rely on nightly quality.
 * Accepted nightlies set the new baseline for periodics.  This is the data that feeds Component Readiness.
 * Every sprint we select a payload for our Engineering Candidate.  This is a public release that partners other dependent teams rely on.
 * After branching we generate release candidates from accepted nightlies.

Going long periods of time without accepted nightlies generates ad-hoc communication throughout SHIP. 
 * Without accepted nightlies the last week of the sprint, the TRT has to scramble to find some way to manually accept a nightly.  This happens often and usually involved 5+ people talking for ~30 minutes plus an engineer or two going off on a special mission to debug an urgent but not important problem.
 * One reason it's urgent is that, without ECs, Product Managers come to ART asking which payload contains a feature they want to preview and if it could be made public.

 * Dramatically increasing nightly build frequency to give us more chances for success
 * Removing low value testing from nightlies
 * Moving more testing to CI payloads (could improve Component Readiness speed)
 * Having a convenient “retry all tests for this payload”
 * Having more advanced ways to revert to the Last Known Good point in time and giving the freedom to fix the problem according to their schedule.
 * Keep identifying and eliminating sources of instability in our CI platform.  We have better data than ever for doing this.

 * Why is it so hard to know who works on what when you really do need a human?

 ## Sustaining the OpenShift Component Readiness triage and remediation is a 50/50 split between OpenShift and SHIP developers taking no more than 20% of TRT time.

 ### Ticket Backlog
 ### Average Ticket Resolution

 ### We'll have metrics on time saved waiting for important things like new repository provisioning.

The overwhelming majority of what SHIP does contributes to the Success Criteria mentioned above.  If you subscribe to this Outcome you’ll be treated to a weekly update on our progress.

 *** Having more TRT engineers on forward thinking projects instead of firefighting will allow us to improve the tooling that helps engineers to understand the CI signal.  The key is making the tooling effective enough that it’s used throughout the entire development cycle (not just reluctantly a few frantic weeks before a big release).

 ** Our progress towards having 95% of tests live where their corresponding features live.
 ** Popular AI tools will even know how add-on components are tested on OpenShift.  If there is any doubt, leaders will ask them where the tests are and what features are covered and what the CI results mean.
 ** Confidence in test coverage leads us to remove all human intervention for releases that pass tests.

h3. *Feature Overview*

Konflux is equal parts powerful release platform and perceived release obstacle.  That apparent contradiction is due to toil that shifted from release engineers to software engineers. The toil has always been there, it’s just only now we feel it acutely.


This presents an opportunity.  We can make the toil go back to the depths from which it came.  With the OCP Konflux migration we’ve proven anything can be automated.  Many teams would love the same Konflux automation and we plan to bring it to them in the name of Delivering Value Daily.

h3. *Goals*

* Less than 2% of engineer time under [~accountid:70121:5777d186-c66a-4037-b13f-2e2c6de8ba27] should be spent doing anything with Konflux.
* Exponential migration to the ART Konflux pipeline over the next 18 months.
** Part of this effort is to give teams hope that relief is coming.
** It took 18 months for OpenShift to migrate and about 3 for ODAP (our first Virt project).  A collection of Logging components will take a little over that.  We expect the pace to increase as we automate more of the common edge cases.
* If we discover any new component’s migration is even half as complex as OpenShift’s we’ll reset and address it with the Konflux team directly as a separate project.

h3. *Requirements*

* We must hire to make this possible.  There aren’t any ARTists sitting around with nothing important to automate today.  To reach the scale we’re targeting we need to hire two more people.  We’re targeting 4-to-5 full time people migrating Hybrid Platforms components to our pipeline.

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*

* How much involvement should we expect from development teams?
** For example, we've had a member of the autoscaling team reach out to us and say they would do everything the ART way if we had time to show them how.
** ART is working on creating AI skill to automate some of the onboarding work, this will make things faster. Here is the Jira for that ART-14718

h3. *Out of Scope*

* Trying to improve the manual Konflux experience for everyone.  
** It’s simply outside of our skillset.  We have _less_ experience with the manual workflow than Hybrid Platforms teams.

h3. *Background*

* [SHIP Konflux Migration|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yV3yNcafmloRgy-7OuIF2dDdIAghL74J8dRBZTLSnbI/edit?slide=id.g2795d4c064f_0_0#slide=id.g2795d4c064f_0_0]

h3. *Customer Considerations*

*How will development teams request inclusion in our Konflux pipeline?*

* We’ll soon have a clear, single support channel for anything related to SHIP.  That will be the medium-term solution.  While we’re still ramping ART up for this project we will approach senior leaders in Hybrid Platforms to learn which teams are facing the most Konflux toil.  This is how OADP and Logging were selected.

*Likewise, how are requests prioritized?*

# Degree of similarity to components already automated (OCP, OADP, Logging).  The more similar, the higher the chance of being selected.
## There is a time-value for this project.  Until a project is automated this effort has zero value to the development team.  If a choice has to be made to pur four people on a single large migration that will take nine months vs four lower-impact but smaller migrations in parallel that will each finish in three, we’re going to pick the latter in the early stages of this effort.
## At first this seems to contradict our desired exponential growth, however, any larger effort that is delayed will benefit from the new tools and patterns we create on smaller projects.
# Customer demand
## Not every team needs to ship every day or every week.  For those that do, our Konflux pipeline is worth the effort.
# Demonstrated high level of toil
## With our emphasis on tracking Activity Types in Jira and other teams metrics available it should be possible to make a case that some toil is more costly than others.  We’re going to prioritize the most expensive forms of toil (complex manual processes for teams that need to ship regularly)
# Stable build processes
## Stable components are a good fit for automation.  Specifically, if a component is already building and releasing manually on Konflux it's typically a good fit for moving to the ART pipeline.  If a component’s build process will significantly change due between in the first 6 months of 2026, it would not be selected for the initial migration.

*Who will make the decision?*

In the early stages of this effort it will likely be a mixture of Justin Pierce, Vikas Laad and Ashwin Das.  By the end of Q2 2026 we’ll have this down to a single person since we hope to be moving much more quickly by that time.

*Where can I see the prioritized list?*

Right here:

# -OADP-
# -Logging-
# -MTC-
# -MTA-
# agent-installer-utils ABI ISO build
# cert-manager Operator for Red Hat OpenShift
# External Secrets Operator for Red Hat OpenShift
# Zero Trust Workload Identity Manager
# ACM
# ACS
# Quay
# <WISH YOU WERE HERE>

 

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

A significant part of speeding this process up involves improving our collaboration with development teams.  You can expect AI assisted support and documentation to play a role.  After our first few successful migrations, subsequent component teams should expect to receive documentation at the start of the project on what we need from them to speed the process along.  Some of this may be able to happen in parallel, meaning, even though ARTists can’t start yet, any prep work needed from development teams could already be done just-in-time.
